title: Should I use my CPA or a specialist for R&D tax credits?
description: Pairing a specialist's R&D documentation with the CPA's return-level elections and filing often works best for the federal credit under IRC § 41.
summary: Should a U.S. business use its CPA or a specialist for the federal R&D tax credit under IRC §41? Because eligibility turns on technical substantiation, pairing a specialist's documentation with the CPA's return-level elections and filing often works best, especially for large claims, client-funded research, amended returns and mandatory Form 6765 Section G reporting from 2026 tax years.

body.text: Should a U.S. business use its CPA or a specialist for the federal R&D tax credit under IRC §41? Because eligibility turns on technical substantiation, pairing a specialist's documentation with the CPA's return-level elections and filing often works best, especially for large claims, client-funded research, amended returns and mandatory Form 6765 Section G reporting from 2026 tax years.
Statements labeled Analysis are interpretation, not statements of law. This report is general information, not tax or legal advice, and it does not create an adviser relationship with any reader.
1. The Short Answer

Analysis. Eligibility under IRC §41(d) turns on scientific and engineering facts; Treas. Reg. §1.41-4(d) requires records detailed enough to substantiate eligibility; and recent Tax Court and Seventh Circuit losses turned on missing technical and time records rather than calculation errors. In 2026 the Tax Court added two further reminders: one that contract terms, and not only engineering facts, can decide whether research is "funded" and therefore excluded, and one that partial substantiation can rescue part of a claim and defeat penalties even when most of it fails.

Whether those facts make a specialist the right choice depends on the size of the claim, the complexity of the research, the business's contract structure, and what documentation the business already keeps. Two reporting changes raise the stakes for the decision now. First, Section G of Form 6765 (business component information) becomes mandatory for tax years beginning after December 31, 2025, subject to exceptions, so most calendar-year filers outside those exceptions will report component-level data for the first time on the 2026 return. Second, the IRS transition period that gives taxpayers 45 days to perfect a deficient research credit refund claim runs only through January 10, 2027.
2. What Is at Stake: The Credit and Its Cash-Flow Features
2.1 The research credit under IRC §41

The credit for increasing research activities is codified at IRC §41. It is computed and claimed on Form 6765, Credit for Increasing Research Activities, which is also used to elect the reduced credit under §280C(c) and to elect the payroll tax application of the credit for qualified small businesses (current Instructions for Form 6765).
The statute provides two computation methods (IRC §41, current text):

items: Regular credit: 20% of qualified research expenses (QREs) above a base amount, plus components for basic research payments and energy research consortium amounts (§41(a)).

Alternative simplified credit (ASC): 14% of QREs above 50% of the average QREs of the three preceding taxable years; 6% of current QREs if the taxpayer had no QREs in any one of those three preceding years (§41(c)(4)).

body.text: The effective percentage depends on the method chosen, the taxpayer's QRE history, and whether the §280C(c) reduced-credit election is made. Under §280C(c) as amended by P.L. 119-21, for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024, a taxpayer that does not elect the reduced credit must reduce its §174A deduction (or the amount charged to capital account) by the full credit amount, while the elected reduced credit is computed by applying the maximum corporate rate to the credit. Either path lowers the net after-tax value below the gross credit, which is one reason the rule of thumb should not be relied on for budgeting. See the hypothetical in Section 2.3.

Analysis. These computation choices are the CPA's natural territory. Choosing between the regular credit and the ASC, modeling the §280C(c) election against the business's projected marginal rate, and coordinating the credit with §174A deductions are return-level decisions that depend on the whole return, not on the technical file. A specialist can supply the QRE figures; the return preparer should own how they flow through the return.
2.2 The qualified small business payroll tax election

items: Gross receipts test: A QSB must have gross receipts of less than $5,000,000 for the taxable year and no gross receipts for any taxable year preceding the five-taxable-year period ending with that year; tax-exempt organizations are excluded (IRC §41(h)(3); Instructions for Form 6765).

Election cap: The election is limited to $250,000, increased by an additional $250,000 for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2022, for a total of $500,000 (IRC §41(h)(4)). Under the Inflation Reduction Act change, the first $250,000 offsets the employer share of Social Security tax and the additional $250,000 can offset the employer share of Medicare tax. The Form 6765 instructions confirm the $500,000 limit on the payroll election.
Number of years: No election may be made once the taxpayer has made the election for five or more preceding taxable years (IRC §41(h)).

How the offset is taken: The elected amount is claimed against payroll taxes on Form 8974, Qualified Small Business Payroll Tax Credit for Increasing Research Activities, attached to the employer's quarterly payroll return, beginning with the first calendar quarter after the income tax return making the election is filed (Instructions for Form 6765; Instructions for Form 8974).

body.text: Where the $31 million figure comes from. $31,000,000 is the inflation-adjusted IRC §448(c) average-annual-gross-receipts threshold applicable to taxable years beginning in 2025. Under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (P.L. 119-21, enacted July 4, 2025) and Rev. Proc. 2025-28 (issued August 28, 2025), small business taxpayers that were not tax shelters and met that test for their first taxable year beginning after December 31, 2024 could elect to apply new §174A (deduction of domestic research or experimental expenditures) retroactively to taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021. That is a deduction rule, not the research credit's QSB definition. Rev. Proc. 2025-28 required the amended-return or administrative adjustment request election to be made by the earlier of July 6, 2026 or the expiration of the §6511 refund period for the year. That window has now closed. A business that missed it can still recover remaining unamortized 2022 through 2024 domestic research expenditures under the catch-up rules Rev. Proc. 2025-28 provides, but not through the small business retroactive election.

Analysis. Confusing the §448(c) threshold with the §41(h) QSB test is exactly the kind of error that matters to the CPA-versus-specialist question. A company with, for example, $12 million of gross receipts might have qualified for the §174A retroactive election but cannot make the payroll tax election at all. Whoever advises the business must keep the two regimes separate, because the payroll election is often the only way a pre-revenue or loss-making company converts the credit into near-term cash.
2.3 Hypothetical: how the effective rate varies

Hypothetical, for illustration only; ignores the §280C(c) reduced-credit election and all other limitations. A company uses the ASC. Current-year QREs are $1,000,000. Average QREs for the prior three years are $800,000.

items: 50% of the three-year average: $800,000 × 50% = $400,000.
Credit as a share of current QREs: $84,000 ÷ $1,000,000 = 8.4%.

body.text: A company with no QREs in one of the prior three years would instead compute $1,000,000 × 6% = $60,000 (6.0%).

Extension of the hypothetical, for illustration only. If the same company makes the §280C(c) reduced-credit election and the maximum corporate rate is 21%, the reduced credit is $84,000 × (1 − 0.21) = $84,000 × 0.79 = $66,360, or 6.6% of current QREs. If instead the company does not elect, it claims the full $84,000 but must reduce its §174A deduction by $84,000; at a 21% marginal rate that reduction costs $84,000 × 21% = $17,640 of tax, for a net benefit of $84,000 − $17,640 = $66,360. In this simplified case the two paths produce the same net benefit; they diverge when the taxpayer's actual marginal rate differs from 21%, when the deduction is not usable in the year, or when the credit is limited by the general business credit rules.

Analysis: the "6% to 8%" range is a plausible gross outcome for many fact patterns, but it is not a fixed rate, and the rate itself is not what a CPA or specialist changes. What changes from one provider to another is which activities and costs are identified and defensibly included as QREs, and that is a documentation question.
2.4 Claiming missed credits on amended returns

A refund claim must generally be filed within 3 years from the time the return was filed or 2 years from the time the tax was paid, whichever period expires later (IRC §6511(a)). The window runs from each return's filing date, and a return filed early is treated as filed on its due date (IRC §6513(a)), so the period does not always equal "the last three years." Amended-return research credit claims are also subject to the specific information requirements described in Section 4.3, and a claim that omits required information during the transition period must be perfected within 45 days of the IRS letter or it is rejected.

Analysis. A rejected claim does not automatically preserve the year. If a claim is rejected close to the end of the §6511 period, a complete new claim may have to be filed before the period expires. Amended research credit claims therefore carry deadline risk as well as substantive risk, and a provider handling them needs both the technical file and a calendar of open years.
3. Why the Credit Is a Technical Question
3.1 The qualification tests
The statute (IRC §41(d)(1)) requires that qualified research:

items: be research with respect to which expenditures may be treated as domestic research or experimental expenditures (the statute now cross-refers to §174A following P.L. 119-21);
be undertaken for the purpose of discovering information that is technological in nature;
be undertaken to discover information the application of which is intended to be useful in the development of a new or improved business component of the taxpayer; and

be research substantially all of the activities of which constitute elements of a process of experimentation for a qualified purpose, meaning a purpose that relates to a new or improved function, performance, reliability or quality, and not to style, taste, cosmetic or seasonal design factors (§41(d)(1), (d)(3)).

body.text: The statute also excludes specific categories, including research after the beginning of commercial production, adaptation and duplication of existing business components, surveys and routine data collection, social science research, research conducted outside the United States, and funded research (IRC §41(d)(4)). Treas. Reg. §1.41-4(a) explains that uncertainty exists when the taxpayer's available information does not establish the capability or method for developing or improving the business component, or its appropriate design, and that a process of experimentation identifies the uncertainty, identifies one or more alternatives intended to eliminate it, and conducts a process of evaluating those alternatives through, for example, modeling, simulation or a systematic trial and error methodology. The regulation applies the "substantially all" requirement at a threshold of 80% or more of the research activities, measured on a cost or other consistently applied reasonable basis (Treas. Reg. §1.41-4(a)(6)), and applies the tests first at the level of the whole business component and then, if the whole component fails, to successively narrower subsets ("shrinking-back," Treas. Reg. §1.41-4(b)(2)).
3.2 Phoenix Design Group, Inc. v. Commissioner

In Phoenix Design Group, Inc. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2024-113 (Docket No. 4759-22, served December 23, 2024), the Tax Court considered research credits that a multidisciplinary engineering consulting firm designing mechanical, electrical, plumbing and fire protection systems had generated in 2013 through 2016 and used in 2015 through 2019. The court found that none of the three sampled projects involved qualified research. It found that the uncertainty the firm described related to components or to owner choices rather than to the basic design of the business component; that routine calculations and expertise-based engineering decisions did not amount to an evaluative process following the scientific method; and that the taxpayer's testimony was sparse and conclusory while its hour sheets were not broken down by design phase or issue. Because the parties had stipulated that penalties would apply if no sampled project qualified, the court held the taxpayer liable for accuracy-related penalties.

The case also has a procedural history that matters for anyone choosing a provider. In an earlier order (August 29, 2023), the Tax Court denied the taxpayer's motion for a protective order that would have limited discovery to a small set of example projects. The practical lesson is that a claim built on a handful of illustrative projects may not survive litigation unless the parties agree that a sample binds all projects or the sample is statistically valid.

Analysis. The firm employed professional engineers, so the problem was not a lack of engineering talent but a lack of records connecting engineering work to an identified uncertainty and an evaluative process. A specialist adds value only if it produces that linkage; credentials alone do not.
3.3 George v. Commissioner

A 2026 Tax Court decision, George v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2026-10, is commonly read alongside Phoenix Design Group. According to published practitioner analysis of the opinion, the taxpayer sustained a portion of the claimed credit, reported as less than 20%, and the accuracy-related penalties were not sustained. The court's discussion drew on the line of cases holding that shortcut estimates of experimentation activities do not suffice without documentation such as records of time spent, and that testimony unsupported by documents may not carry the burden.

Analysis. Read together, Phoenix Design Group and George show the range of outcomes. Where documentation is thin across the board, the credit and penalties can both be lost; where some activities are documented, part of the credit can survive and a reasonable, documented approach can help defeat penalties. That range is the practical measure of what a careful preparer, CPA or specialist, contributes.
4. Documentation: The Core of a Defensible Claim
4.1 The regulatory recordkeeping rule

Treas. Reg. §1.41-4(d) provides that a taxpayer claiming the credit "must retain records in sufficiently usable form and detail to substantiate that the expenditures claimed are eligible for the credit," cross-referencing the general record retention rules of Treas. Reg. §1.6001-1. The regulation does not prescribe a particular format, and the preamble to the 2004 final regulations indicated that taxpayers are not required to keep records beyond those required by §6001, but the burden of substantiation remains on the taxpayer.
4.2 What IRS examiners look for

The IRS Audit Techniques Guide on substantiation and recordkeeping for the credit for increasing research activities (dated June 2005, and stated by the IRS to be accurate only as of that date) lists the records examiners seek. They include project authorizations, budgets or work orders; project summaries, progress reports and meeting minutes; wage data by employee name, amount, percentage of annual wages, department, job title and job description; supplies by category tied to the general ledger; and contract research by counterparty, amount and category. The guide also states that the IRS does not have to accept estimates of QREs and that taxpayers must have factual support for every assumption underlying an estimate.

The principle is consistent with the statute, which defines qualified services by the activity performed (engaging in, directly supervising or directly supporting qualified research) rather than by position (IRC §41(b)(2)(B)), and with Moore (Section 6.2), where records of the executive's role did not establish how much of his time was spent on qualified activities.

Treas. Reg. §1.41-2(c) supplies the definitions that make this activity-based approach concrete. "Engaging in" qualified research means actual conduct of the research; "direct supervision" means the immediate supervision of qualified research, such as by a research scientist directly supervising laboratory scientists, and does not include supervision by a higher-level manager to whom first-line supervisors report; and "direct support" means services in direct support of either persons engaging in or directly supervising qualified research. The regulations also provide that if substantially all (80% or more) of an employee's services are qualified services, all of that employee's wages may be treated as wages for qualified services (Treas. Reg. §1.41-2(d)(2)).
4.3 Refund-claim disclosure (IR-2021-203) and Form 6765 Section G

items: Amended-return refund claims. IR-2021-203 (October 15, 2021) announced that a valid research credit refund claim must include five items of information, effective for claims filed on or after January 10, 2022. Effective for claims postmarked on or after June 18, 2024, the IRS waived two of them (the names of the individuals who performed each research activity and the information each individual sought to discover), while reserving the right to request that information in examination. The remaining requirements are to identify all business components to which the claim relates for that year, identify all research activities performed for each business component, and provide the total qualified employee wage expenses, total qualified supply expenses and total qualified contract research expenses for the claim year, which may be reported on Form 6765. In IR-2025-99 (October 1, 2025) the IRS extended the transition period, during which taxpayers receive a letter and have 45 days to perfect a deficient claim before a final determination, through January 10, 2027. This was the second extension; the period previously ran through January 10, 2026.

Form 6765, Section G (business component information). Per-component QRE reporting is Section G of the redesigned Form 6765. In IR-2025-99 the IRS delayed mandatory Section G reporting by one year. Under the current Instructions for Form 6765, Section G is optional for all filers for tax years beginning before 2026 and is required for tax years beginning after 2025, with two exceptions: a QSB that elects the payroll tax credit, and a filer that reports the credit on an original return and has controlled-group QREs of $1.5 million or less and average annual gross receipts of $50 million or less for the prior three tax years (determined under §448(c)(3)). Sections E (qualitative questions about the business) and F (QRE summary by category) are required of all filers.

body.text: Analysis. For most calendar-year businesses that do not qualify for an exception, the 2026 return (filed in 2027) is the first one on which component-level reporting is mandatory. That is the most concrete current reason a business might move from an informal approach to a structured documentation process, whoever prepares the claim. The small-filer exception is also relevant to the provider decision: it applies only to a credit reported on an original return, so a business that discovers missed credits and claims them on an amended return cannot rely on it. Separately, the January 10, 2027 end of the refund-claim transition period means a business filing amended research credit claims after that date should assume a deficient claim may be rejected outright rather than returned for perfection, unless the IRS extends the period again.
4.4 Estimates and sampling

The IRS Research Credit Claims Audit Techniques Guide (LMSB-04-0508-030, May 2008) instructs examiners that a claim may warrant disallowance or return to the taxpayer if it "relies too heavily on high level estimations (i.e. interviews, estimates, judgment sampling, etc.)." It also states that taxpayers must support 100% of the credit claimed unless a valid statistical sample is used, and that no authority permits judgment sampling to compute the credit.

The Seventh Circuit reinforced the order of proof in Little Sandy Coal Co. v. Commissioner, 62 F.4th 287 (7th Cir. 2023), affirming T.C. Memo. 2021-15. The taxpayer, a shipbuilder, did not document whether hypotheses and alternatives were tested and refined in a scientific manner, and the court explained that only after a taxpayer establishes that qualified research occurred under §41(d) may the amount of QREs be estimated under §41(b) if needed. In Betz v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2023-84, the Tax Court reached different conclusions project by project within a sample and did not accept testimony that was unsupported by documentation. Estimates therefore have a limited role: they may help quantify costs once qualification is proved, but they cannot prove qualification.
5. The Generalist CPA: Role and Limitations
5.1 Where the CPA is indispensable

Form 6765 is used to compute the credit, make the §280C(c) reduced-credit election, and make the QSB payroll election, and the payroll offset is then claimed quarterly on Form 8974 (Instructions for Form 6765). The research credit is a component of the general business credit under IRC §38, so it is subject to the §38(c) limitation based on tax liability, and unused credits generally carry back one year and forward 20 years under IRC §39. Pass-through entities compute the credit at the entity level and allocate it to owners, who claim it on their own returns, and individual owners may be subject to the passive activity and at-risk limits.

Analysis: the §280C(c) election, the payroll election, the §38 limitation and carryover tracking, owner-level effects in pass-through entities, and the §174A treatment of research expenditures are return-level decisions that sit naturally with the business's regular preparer. A specialist that prepares the technical study without coordinating these items can produce a credit the business cannot use efficiently.
5.2 The claimed knowledge and resource gap

Analysis. Because the IRS can decline estimates (Section 4.2) and the courts have disallowed credits for lack of technical and time records (Sections 3.2, 4.4 and 6.2), any preparer, CPA or specialist, needs a method for capturing technical evidence. Whether a particular CPA firm has that method is a question to ask that firm, not something that can be assumed from its being a generalist. Many CPA firms of all sizes operate dedicated research credit practices with engineering staff, and many specialist firms rely on the client's own engineers for the technical facts; the label alone does not tell a business who will actually build its file.
6. The Case for Specialization
6.1 Interdisciplinary review and funded research

Research is not qualified "to the extent funded by any grant, contract, or otherwise by another person (or governmental entity)" (IRC §41(d)(4)(H)). Under Treas. Reg. §1.41-4A(d), which applies to current years through the cross-reference in Treas. Reg. §1.41-4(a), amounts payable under an agreement are treated as funding unless they are contingent on the success of the research, and a taxpayer that retains no substantial rights in the research is treated as fully funded; a taxpayer does not retain substantial rights if it must pay for the right to use the results.

The Tax Court applied these rules to an architecture firm in Smith v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2026-50 (filed June 16, 2026). The taxpayers were the partners of Adrian Smith + Gordon Gill Architecture, LLP, an Illinois firm that designs large-scale and highly technical buildings, and the credits related to its 2008 through 2010 tax years. The IRS conceded that the work met the §41(d) qualification tests, so the dispute centered on whether client contracts made the research "funded" and on whether the partners' compensation was reasonable under §174(e). The court held that the firm retained substantial rights in its research, but that it could claim credits only to the extent its research expenses exceeded the payments it received; it found the fixed-fee, milestone-based contracts more closely resembled those in Meyer, Borgman & Johnson, Inc. v. Commissioner, 100 F.4th 986 (8th Cir. 2024), where payment was not contingent on success. The court also rejected the taxpayers' argument, made under Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo (2024), that the funded-research regulations are invalid, and evaluated the partners' compensation using the independent investor test of Exacto Spring Corp. v. Commissioner, 196 F.3d 833 (7th Cir. 1999).

Analysis. Smith shows that for a firm doing client work, the credit can turn on contract terms reviewed under local law even when the engineering plainly qualifies. That review requires both contract-reading skill and knowledge of the funded-research case law (Fairchild Industries, Dynetics, Meyer, Borgman & Johnson, System Technologies and now Smith). A business with significant client-funded work should ask any provider who will review its contracts, under what state's law, and how payment terms and intellectual property clauses will be analyzed before the credit is claimed.
6.2 Lessons from Moore v. Commissioner

The dispute concerned whether the wages of one executive could be included in QREs. Nevco, Inc., an S corporation that makes scoreboards and related equipment, claimed research credits for 2014 and 2015 that flowed through to its shareholder and her spouse. They treated the salary and bonus of Nevco's president and chief operating officer as wages for qualified services. The Tax Court (T.C. Memo. 2023-20, Docket No. 18632-19, February 23, 2023) held that his wages could not be included, because the record provided no basis to determine what portion of his time was spent conducting or directly supervising qualified research as distinguished from broader new-product work, and his supervision of first-line supervisors was not direct supervision within Treas. Reg. §1.41-2(c)(2). The Seventh Circuit affirmed (Moore v. Commissioner, 101 F.4th 509 (7th Cir. 2024), No. 23-2681, decided April 30, 2024), treating the Tax Court's conclusion as a finding of fact reviewed for clear error and noting the absence of written records of how he spent his time, which Treas. Reg. §1.41-4(d) requires, and that he could not estimate his qualified time even approximately. The IRS had been willing to treat the salary of the company's director of engineering as a qualified research expense; the dispute concerned the COO. The case concerned the COO's wages, not the company's entire credit.

Analysis. Moore is a time-tracking case, not an engineering-expertise case. It also shows where claims tend to be weakest: owners and executives whose wages are large and whose time is divided between management and technical work.
6.3 Methodology and maximization

Analysis. A claim that is larger because more activities were identified is only an improvement if those activities can be substantiated under the standards in Sections 3 and 4. When comparing proposals, a business should ask each provider to explain, for the largest business components, what uncertainty it will document, what records will show the process of experimentation, and how wages will be tied to qualified activities, rather than comparing projected credit amounts.
7. Audit and Penalty Exposure
7.1 Does claiming the credit trigger an audit?

Aprio's list is: scrutiny of another area of the return, an audit of a related party, operating in an industry of IRS focus, exceptionally high credit amounts, beginning to claim credits after a period of net operating losses, and claiming a refund on an amended return.

Analysis. The redesigned Form 6765, with mandatory Sections E and F and, from 2026, Section G, gives the IRS more structured information on every return that claims the credit. Whatever the selection method, the information a business reports on the form is now more detailed and easier to compare against its later examination file, so inconsistencies between the form and the underlying study are more likely to be noticed.
7.2 The accuracy-related penalty
IRS, "Accuracy-related penalty," last reviewed October 15, 2026; IRC §6662:

items: The penalty is 20% of the portion of an underpayment attributable to, among other things, negligence or disregard of rules or regulations, or a substantial understatement of income tax (IRC §6662(a), (b)).

A corporation (other than an S corporation or personal holding company) has a substantial understatement when the understatement exceeds the lesser of 10% of the tax required to be shown on the return (or, if greater, $10,000) or $10,000,000 (IRC §6662(d)(1)(B)). For other taxpayers, the threshold is the greater of 10% of the tax required to be shown or $5,000.
Negligence includes any failure to make a reasonable attempt to comply with the tax laws (IRC §6662(c)).
No penalty applies to any portion of an underpayment for which the taxpayer shows reasonable cause and good faith (IRC §6664(c)).

body.text: Phoenix Design Group (Section 3.2) is a reminder that penalties can accompany a disallowed research credit; there, they applied by stipulation. George (Section 3.3) shows the contrasting outcome, where penalties were not sustained.

Hypothetical, for illustration only. A C corporation's $84,000 credit (from Section 2.3) is fully disallowed, producing an $84,000 understatement. Tax required to be shown is $500,000. Threshold: 10% × $500,000 = $50,000, which exceeds $10,000 and is less than $10,000,000, so the threshold is $50,000. Because $84,000 exceeds $50,000, the understatement is substantial. Penalty: $84,000 × 20% = $16,800, plus repayment of the $84,000 and interest (not computed). Reasonable-cause and other defenses are not considered here.

Variation, for illustration only. If only $40,000 of the same credit were disallowed, the understatement of $40,000 would not exceed the $50,000 threshold, so the substantial-understatement penalty would not apply, although the IRS could still assert the negligence penalty if the facts supported it. If the penalty did apply on that basis, it would be $40,000 × 20% = $8,000.

Whether reasonable cause exists depends on the facts of each case, including the taxpayer's efforts to determine its proper liability and, where reliance on an adviser is asserted, whether the adviser was competent, had all the necessary facts, and whether the taxpayer relied on the advice in good faith (Treas. Reg. §1.6664-4(b), (c)).
7.3 Study and defense costs
Fee structures in this market include fixed fees, hourly billing and contingent fees calculated as a percentage of the credit.

Analysis. Fee structure is relevant to the CPA-versus-specialist decision. CPAs and other practitioners who represent taxpayers before the IRS are subject to professional rules on contingent fees, including the AICPA Code of Professional Conduct and Treasury Department Circular 230, §10.27, and the scope of those rules for refund claims has been the subject of litigation. A business evaluating a contingent-fee proposal from any provider should ask how the fee will be calculated if the credit is later reduced or disallowed on examination, whether any part of the fee is refundable in that case, and whether the provider has confirmed that the arrangement complies with the professional rules that apply to it.
8. Evaluating a Specialist

cells: Exclusive focus on R&D tax credits; presence in all 50 states
The firm's own statement (About Us page).
"ISO 31000:2009 Risk Management" certification confirming the firm's risk-management processes

The firm lists ISO 31000:2009, but ISO states that ISO 31000 cannot be used for certification purposes; it is a guidance standard. ISO 31000:2009 has also been superseded by ISO 31000:2018. The "certification" framing is inaccurate.
The firm lists ISO 27001 (no edition or certificate number given).
IRS-approved continuing-education provider for Enrolled Agents
NASBA National Registry lists the firm (Registry ID 139434).
"Six-Eye Review" of every claim by a qualified engineer, a scientist, and a CPA or Enrolled Agent
The firm's described internal process (About Us; Audit Defense page; NASBA registry profile).
TaxTrex AI analyzes survey text and keywords to assess claim risk before finalization
The firm's description. The firm presents TaxTrex as a self-claim tool it says takes about 90 minutes. The Audit Defense page states that TaxTrex and other software or services are not free.
creditARMOR "includes insurance coverage" for defense costs, including CPA, tax attorney and consultant fees

The firm's Audit Defense page describes creditARMOR as an AI-assisted mock audit and audit-management platform and states that no insurance policy, reimbursement benefit, or financial indemnity is offered through that page, and that there is no promise to pay losses or to provide services if a future audit occurs. Its pro bono offer covers only the firm's own audit services, without professional service fees, for an existing examination where the claim passed the creditARMOR mock audit and the firm confirmed the passing result in writing. It excludes third-party CPA or attorney fees, taxes, interest, penalties, denied credits and other financial losses; excludes appeals and litigation unless expressly included in writing; does not reserve help for future audits; and does not make the mock audit fee free. The firm's About Us page uses the phrase "help insure"; the more specific Audit Defense disclaimer controls.
Comparison table: audit defense "included"; defense fees "covered and managed by structured defense programs"
Coverage is limited to the firm's own services under stated conditions.

body.text: Analysis. A business comparing providers should get the scope of any audit-defense commitment in writing, including whether it covers third-party fees, appeals, penalties and interest, and whether it applies to future examinations or only to an existing one, rather than relying on marketing summaries. The same diligence applies to any firm, specialist or CPA: credentials should be checked against the issuing body's own registry, and "certification" claims should be checked against whether the standard is certifiable at all.
9. The Recommended Model: CPA and Specialist Together

Analysis. Return-level elections (§280C(c), the QSB payroll election, §174A treatment), the §38 limitation and carryovers, owner-level effects, and Form 6765 filing belong with the preparer of the return. The evidence the law demands (identification of business components and uncertainty, a documented process of experimentation, activity-level time records, contract review for funded research, and from 2026 Section G component reporting) is where specialized technical input adds most value.

Analysis. Three situations make the case for adding specialized technical help strongest: claims large enough that Section G applies and the small-filer exception does not; businesses whose research is performed under client contracts, where Smith shows that contract terms can decide the outcome; and amended-return claims, which must meet the refund-claim information requirements and cannot use the Section G small-filer exception. Conversely, a business with modest, well-documented internal research, an experienced CPA with a defined research credit method, and QREs under the Section G exception thresholds may reasonably keep the work with its CPA. In every case, the two advisers should agree in advance on who owns the technical file, who signs off on the Form 6765 figures, and who will respond if the IRS examines the claim.
9.1 Questions to ask either provider (Analysis)

items: How will you identify each business component and document the technical uncertainty and the alternatives evaluated, given Phoenix Design Group?
How will you capture each employee's time on qualified activities, including owners and executives, given Moore and Treas. Reg. §1.41-4(d)?

Will the method rely on interviews and estimates, or on contemporaneous records and, where used, a valid statistical sample, given Little Sandy Coal and the Research Credit Claims Audit Techniques Guide?

Are you prepared to complete Form 6765 Section G for 2026 tax years, and to meet the refund-claim information requirements for any amended returns, including before the January 10, 2027 end of the transition period?
Who reviews customer and grant contracts for the funded-research exclusion, and how will payment terms and intellectual property rights be analyzed, given Smith?
How will the credit be coordinated with the §280C(c) election, §174A deductions, the §38 limitation and, for pass-through entities, owner-level limits?
How is your fee calculated, and how does it change if the credit is reduced on examination?
Exactly what does any audit-support commitment cover, and what does it exclude?

body.text: 10. Conclusion

That favors involving technical expertise, often through a specialist working with the business's CPA, especially for larger or more complex claims, for businesses doing client-funded work, and for the mandatory Section G reporting that begins with tax years beginning after 2025. The choice is best made on the specific provider's documentation method, contract-review capability, coordination with the return preparer, and written commitments rather than on the generalist-versus-specialist label alone.
